items.subject: patterns
items.title: Pattern train
items.summary: Patterns repeat. Can you make one?
steps: 🔴🔵🔴🔵 Look! Red, blue, red, blue.
🧦 Line up big things: sock, spoon, sock, spoon.
❓ What comes next?
🚂 Make your own pattern train.
👏 Ask a grown-up to guess what comes next!

hazards: Small objects can be a choking risk
safety.notes: Use objects bigger than the child's fist. An adult stays nearby.

basic.description: Make patterns with things from home.

better.description: Cut big paper squares and make colour patterns.

advanced.description: Build patterned towers with large blocks.

substitutions.use: Leaves and stones (big ones) or socks and spoons

items.subject: sequences
items.title: Be a robot
items.summary: Robots follow instructions exactly. Can you?
steps: 🤖 You are the robot!
⬆️ Grown-up says "step forward".
↩️ "Turn." ⬆️ "Step, step."
🧸 Can the robot reach the teddy?
🔄 Swap! Now you give the instructions.

safety.notes: Clear a space and walk slowly. Small steps only.

materials: A teddy or toy as the goal
basic.description: Give spoken instructions to reach the toy.

better.description: Draw arrow cards ⬆️ ↩️ ↪️ and lay them in a line as the program.

advanced.description: Tape a grid on the floor and plan the whole route before the robot moves.

substitutions.use: Floor tiles, a rug pattern or chalk outside

items.adultNote: Follow the instructions exactly as given, even when they are "wrong" - that is the fun and the lesson.

items.subject: online safety
items.title: Ask a grown-up first
items.summary: Before you tap or play online, ask a grown-up.
steps: 📱 Want to use a phone or tablet? Ask first.
🙋 Something pops up? Show a grown-up.
🤐 Your name and home are private.
😟 Feel funny or scared? Tell a grown-up straight away.
👍 You will not be in trouble for telling.

check.question: A game asks where you live. What do you do?
check.explain: Yes! Ask a grown-up. Where you live is private.

items.adultNote: Agree simple family rules now (where devices are used, for how long). Children who are not punished for telling keep telling.

items.subject: algorithms
items.title: Arrow maze treasure hunt
items.summary: Write a program of arrows to guide a character to the treasure.
steps: Draw a 5 x 5 grid on paper.
Put a smiley in one corner and a treasure in another.
Draw a few walls the character cannot pass.
Write the program as arrows: ➡️ ➡️ ⬇️ ...
Ask someone to follow your arrows with a finger.
Did it work? If not, find the wrong arrow and fix it. That is called debugging!

check.question: Your program goes the wrong way. What is fixing it called?
check.explain: Yes! Every programmer debugs. Mistakes help us learn.

items.subject: how computers work
items.title: Input, process, output
items.summary: A computer takes in information, does something with it, and gives an answer.
steps: Input: information goes in, like pressing keys, touching a screen or speaking.
Process: the computer follows instructions (a program) very fast.
Output: something comes out, like a picture, a sound or words.
Storage: computers can save information to use later.
Computers are everywhere: phones, washing machines, cars, calculators.
Find three machines at home that have a tiny computer inside. Name their inputs and outputs.

check.question: A microphone is...
check.explain: Yes. It takes sound into the device.

check.question: A speaker is...
check.explain: Yes. Sound comes out of it.

items.subject: online safety
items.title: A stranger in the game chat
items.summary: Someone you do not know sends you a message in a game. What do you do?
steps: Read the messages.
Choose the safest answer.
Talk about it with a trusted adult.

safety.notes: A pretend scenario. If a real message ever worries the child, an adult should help report and block.

simulation.scenario: You are playing an online game. A player you do not know writes: "Hi! You're really good. What school do you go to?"

options.text: Do not answer the question, and tell a trusted adult
options.feedback: Great. Your school, home and full name are private.
That is private information. Strangers online may not be who they say.

steps.prompt: They write: "Don't tell your parents, it's our secret. Send me a photo."

options.text: Stop chatting, block them and show an adult right away
options.feedback: Exactly right. Asking for secrets and photos is a warning sign.

options.text: Send a photo but keep it a secret
options.feedback: Never. A safe person never asks a child to keep secrets from their family.

steps.prompt: You feel worried you will be in trouble. Should you still tell?

options.text: Yes - telling is always the right thing
options.feedback: Yes. You have done nothing wrong by telling.
Please still tell an adult. They can help report the person.

items.adultNote: Reassure the child they will not lose devices for telling you. Know how to block and report in the apps your child uses.

items.subject: loops
items.title: Loop dance
items.summary: A loop repeats steps. Make a dance program with loops!
steps: Choose 3 moves: clap 👏, jump ⬆️, spin 🔄.
Write a dance: clap, clap, clap, clap, jump.
Now write it shorter with a loop: REPEAT 4 [clap], jump.
Make a longer dance that uses two loops.
Ask someone to "run" your dance program.
Bonus: add a condition: IF the music stops THEN freeze.

safety.notes: Clear a space. Keep spins slow and stop if dizzy.

basic.description: Write the dance program on paper and perform it.

better.description: Play music and add "IF music stops THEN freeze".

advanced.description: Program a cartoon character to do the same dance with loop blocks.

substitutions.use: A phone or tablet browser with a free coding website

items.subject: cybersecurity
items.title: Super-strong passwords
items.summary: A strong password keeps your accounts safe. Learn the three-random-words trick.
steps: Weak passwords are short or easy to guess, like "123456" or your pet's name.
Strong idea: join three random words, for example "teapot-river-violin" (do not use this one!).
Longer is stronger. Add a number or symbol if a site asks.
Use a different password for every important account, especially email.
Never share passwords with friends. Trusted adults can help you store them safely.
Turn on two-step checks (a code sent to a trusted device) when an adult helps you set up an account.
Practise: make three pretend passwords on paper and rate them weak, OK or strong. Then tear up the paper.

check.question: Which is stronger?
check.explain: Yes. Longer, random words are much harder to guess.

check.question: Should you use the same password everywhere?
options: No, one leak would unlock everything
check.explain: Use a different one for each important account.

items.subject: AI literacy
items.title: What is AI (and what is it not)?
items.summary: AI is computer software that learns patterns from lots of examples. It is useful, but it is not magic and it can be wrong.
steps: AI stands for artificial intelligence.
Many AI tools are trained on huge amounts of examples (data) and learn patterns from them.
AI can recognise faces, translate languages, suggest videos or write text.
AI is NOT a person. It does not have feelings, and it does not truly know you.
AI can be wrong. It can make up facts that sound confident. Always check important things.
AI can be unfair if its training examples were unfair.
Never tell an AI chatbot your full name, address, school, passwords or photos of yourself.
Find three places AI might be used in your life. Are they helpful? What could go wrong?

check.question: An AI chatbot gives you a fact for homework. What should you do?
options: Check it in another reliable source
check.explain: Yes. AI can sound sure and still be wrong.

check.question: Does an AI chatbot have feelings?
check.explain: No. It can copy the way people talk, but it does not feel.

items.adultNote: Check the age rules of any AI tool before your child uses it, and supervise use.

items.subject: AI literacy
items.title: Train a pretend AI
items.summary: Be the AI! Learn from examples, then see what happens when the examples are not fair.
steps: Draw 12 small cards: 6 fruits and 6 vegetables (or animals that fly / do not fly).
Teacher shows you 8 cards with labels. That is your "training data".
Write your rule: how do you tell them apart?
Teacher shows the last 4 cards without labels. Use your rule to guess.
How many did you get right? That is your "accuracy".
Now try again, but the training cards are only red fruits. Does your rule work for a banana?
Talk: if training data leaves things out, AI can make unfair mistakes.

items.subject: data
items.title: Favourite fruit survey
items.summary: Collect data, make a chart and find out what it tells you.
steps: Choose a question, like "What is your favourite fruit?"
Ask at least 8 people (family, neighbours with an adult, or friends by phone).
Record answers with tally marks: draw four lines, then cross them with a fifth line. That bundle counts as 5.
Draw a bar chart on paper: one bar for each answer.
Write two sentences: what is most popular? What surprised you?
Think: would the answer change if you asked different people?

check.question: A bundle of 5 (four lines crossed by a fifth), then ||| more. How many?
check.explain: The bundle is 5 plus 3 more makes 8.

items.subject: programming
items.title: Build a guess-the-number game
items.summary: Build a simple program: the computer picks a secret number and gives hints until you guess it.
steps: Plan on paper first: what does the program need to do?
Step 1: pick a secret number from 1 to 20 and store it in a variable.
Step 2: ask the player for a guess.
Step 3: IF guess is too high, say "Lower". IF too low, say "Higher".
Step 4: REPEAT until the guess is right, then say "You got it!"
Build it with block coding or text coding, or run it on paper with a friend as the computer.
Test it. Find and fix bugs. Then add a guess counter.

safety.notes: Take a break from screens every 30 minutes.

basic.description: Write the program as a flow chart. One person is the "computer" and follows it exactly.

better.description: Snap blocks together for variables, loops and "if" blocks.

advanced.description: Type the program in a beginner text language and add a score.

substitutions.use: Paper and pencil: write the program and run it by hand, step by step
A phone or tablet browser with a free coding website
Roll dice or pick a numbered card

items.adultNote: Many free, reputable coding sites run in a phone browser without installing anything. Check privacy settings and do not let the child create accounts without you.

items.subject: cybersecurity
items.title: Is this message a trick?
items.summary: Scammers send fake messages to steal passwords or money. Can you spot them?
steps: Read each message.
Decide what is safe.
Look for warning signs.

safety.notes: Pretend messages only. Never click links in real suspicious messages.

simulation.scenario: You get a message: "URGENT! Your game account will be deleted in 1 hour. Click here and enter your password to keep it."

steps.prompt: What is the biggest warning sign?

options.text: It rushes you and asks for your password
options.feedback: Yes. Pressure plus a password request is a classic trick.
Scammers often mention things you use to look real. Look for rushing and requests.

options.text: Do not click. Open the game the normal way to check, and tell an adult
options.feedback: Perfect. Go to the real site or app yourself.

options.text: Click the link quickly before it is too late
options.feedback: The hurry is part of the trick. Real companies do not ask for your password like this.

steps.prompt: A message says you won a prize but must pay a small fee first. This is...

options.feedback: Right. Real prizes do not ask you to pay first.
Be careful. "Pay to get a prize" is a common scam.

items.subject: digital wellbeing
items.title: My screen balance plan
items.summary: Screens can be fun and useful. A good plan leaves time for sleep, people and moving.
steps: For 3 days, write down roughly when and why you use screens.
Sort each use: learning, making, chatting, relaxing or just scrolling.
Notice: how did you feel after each type?
Make a plan: screen-free times (meals, the hour before bed), and things you want more of.
Use helpful settings: turn off non-urgent notifications, keep devices out of the bedroom at night.
Review the plan with a family member after a week.
items.adultNote: Make a family plan rather than a rule just for the child. Adults modelling the plan makes it work.

items.subject: networks
items.title: How does the internet work?
items.summary: The internet is a giant network of computers that pass small packets of data to each other.
steps: Your message is split into small pieces called packets.
Each packet has an address, like a letter. Computers on the internet have IP addresses.
Routers pass packets along, often taking different paths, then they are put back together.
DNS works like a phone book: it turns a website name into an address.
The padlock in a browser means the connection is encrypted: scrambled so others cannot read it.
Unplugged demo: write a sentence on 5 numbered slips, pass them around a room in random order, then rebuild the sentence.

check.question: What does DNS do?
check.explain: Yes. It is like a phone book for the internet.

items.subject: programming
items.title: Code a program that solves a real problem
items.summary: Plan, build and test a program that helps someone, like a budget tracker, a quiz or a chore rota.
steps: Interview a "user" (a family member): what problem would they like solved?
Write the requirements: what must it do? What would be nice?
Design: draw the screens or text prompts, and a flow chart.
Build a small working version first, then add features.
Test with real users. Write down every bug and fix it.
Write short instructions for the user and comments in your code.
Reflect: what would you build next?

safety.notes: Take regular breaks. Do not collect real personal details; use pretend data.

basic.description: Design the program fully on paper with pseudocode and a hand-run test table.

better.description: Write and run short programs in a mobile browser.

advanced.description: Build a fuller program and save it in a project folder.

substitutions.use: Paper and pencil: write the program and run it by hand, step by step
A phone or tablet browser with a free coding website

items.subject: robotics
items.title: Design a helper robot
items.summary: Robots sense, think and act. Design a robot that solves a small problem.
steps: Pick a problem, like watering a plant when soil is dry.
Sense: what sensor does it need? (soil moisture, light, distance)
Think: write the program as IF... THEN... rules.
Act: what moves or changes? (a pump, a motor, a light)
Build a cardboard model and label each part.
Advanced: with an adult, build a working version with a low-cost microcontroller kit.
Present your robot and explain its sense-think-act loop.

safety.notes: An adult supervises cutting and any electronics. Use low-voltage battery kits only, never mains electricity. Disconnect batteries when not in use.

basic.description: Build a model robot and write its program on paper.

better.description: Make a simple circuit that turns a motor or light on with a switch.

advanced.description: Program a real sensor to control a motor or light.

substitutions.use: A cardboard model and a paper program
Some boards can be programmed from a phone browser

sources.title: Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents

items.adultNote: Keep to low-voltage kits. Coin and button batteries are dangerous if swallowed: keep them away from younger siblings.

items.subject: AI literacy
items.title: Using AI tools wisely
items.summary: AI tools can help you learn, but they can also mislead you. Use them like a clever but unreliable helper.
steps: Use AI to explain, quiz you or give feedback, not to do your thinking for you.
Be honest: say when you used AI in your work.
Check facts, numbers and quotes against reliable sources. AI can invent sources.
Ask: whose data trained this? Who might it treat unfairly?
Deepfakes are fake pictures, voices or videos made with AI. Check before you believe or share.
Privacy: never enter personal details, other people's information or passwords.
Try it: ask an AI tool (with an adult) a question you already know the answer to. Was it right?

check.question: An AI tool gives you a source for an essay. You should...
options: find and read the source yourself
check.explain: AI can make up sources that do not exist.

items.adultNote: Check the minimum age and privacy terms of any AI service. The offline version: discuss real examples from news on paper.
